title: Cameron: love for the gifts is human; God's love makes the gifts
source_text: XI. Et similiter Camero in jam supra memorata digressione de gratia, Caeterum, inquit, observandum est dona Dei nunquam dici hoc sensu gratiam, quasi iis conciliaretur Dei favor, eaque dona nos redderent Deo gratos & acceptos. Sed si quando dona Dei dicuntur gratia hoc sensu, hominum ratio habetur, qui istis donis inducuntur in amorem, non autem habetur ratio Dei. Quod ut percipiatur intelligendum est humanum amorem qui conciliatur istis donis, non efficere haec dona, sed invenire. At amor divinus idem invenit & effecit haec dona: ut pictor qui delectatur opere suo, idem gaudet pulchritudine operis, & autor fuit istius pulchritudinis. Itaque nulla debuit dici gratia gratum faciens proprie loquendo, sed potius dicenda fuit illa gratia gratum facientis.
pass_a_gloss: XI. And similarly Cameron in the digression on grace already mentioned above, But, he says, it is to be observed that the gifts of God are never called grace in this sense, as though by them the favour of God were won, and those gifts rendered us pleasing and accepted to God. But if ever the gifts of God are called grace in this sense, account is had of men, who are induced into love by those gifts, but account is not had of God. That this may be perceived it is to be understood that human love which is won by those gifts, does not make these gifts, but finds them. But divine love the same both found and made these gifts: as a painter who delights in his work, the same rejoices in the beauty of the work, and was the author of that beauty. Therefore no grace ought to have been called making pleasing properly speaking, but rather that ought to have been called the grace of one making pleasing.
pass_b_english: Thesis XI. Cameron says much the same in the digression on grace mentioned above. It must be noted, he writes, that God's gifts are never called grace in the sense that they win God's favour, as if those gifts made us pleasing and acceptable to God.

If God's gifts are ever called grace in that sense, the reference is to human beings, who are drawn to love by such gifts, and not to God. To see this, one must understand that human love won by these gifts does not make the gifts but finds them. Divine love both found and made them, like a painter who delights in his work: he takes joy in its beauty and was also the one who produced that beauty.
So, strictly speaking, no grace should have been called grace that makes pleasing. It should rather have been called the grace of the one who makes pleasing.

choices.why: The scholastic pair (Aquinas, Summa theologiae I-II q. 111 a. 1): gifts given for the good of others versus the grace that makes its bearer pleasing to God. Kept literal because the Reformed objections turn on the very words.
